title: Broken Link Building: A Step-by-Step Outreach Process
excerpt: Find dead links on resource pages, learn what they covered, offer a better replacement and write an outreach email that gets read, without turning into spam.
meta_title: Broken Link Building: A Step-by-Step Outreach Guide
meta_description: A practical broken link building process: find resource pages, crawl for dead links, check the Wayback Machine, build a replacement and email politely.
key_takeaways: Broken link building works because you start by reporting a real problem on someone else's site and offering a useful fix.
Resource pages on schools, clubs, associations and established blogs are the best places to look for dead outbound links.
Crawling resource pages and checking outbound status codes finds 404s and dead domains far faster than clicking links by hand.
The Wayback Machine shows what a dead page used to cover, so your replacement can match or beat it without copying it.
Send short, individual emails, follow up only once, and never pay or trade for the link.
content_html:
Resource pages rot. A city council publishes a "home composting resources" page, links to a dozen helpful guides, and then nobody touches it for three years. Some of those guides move, some sites shut down, and the page quietly fills with dead links. For broken link building, that neglect is an opportunity.

Now say you run a site about home composting, and you have a thorough guide that covers the same ground as one of those dead links. The page owner has a problem (a broken link that frustrates their readers) and you have a fix. That is broken link building in one sentence.

Done well, it is one of the few outreach tactics where you lead with something useful instead of a request. Done badly, it is just another spam email.

This guide walks through the full process: finding the right pages, checking links at scale, working out what the dead page covered, building a replacement, writing an email people actually read, and tracking it all. If you are new to link building in general, our no-nonsense guide to off-page SEO covers why links matter in the first place.

Why broken link building works

Most outreach asks a stranger for a favor. Broken link building starts by doing them one: you have found an error on their site and you are telling them about it.

The link is a by-product of a genuinely helpful report, which is why it gets better responses than a cold "please link to us".

It also stays on the right side of Google's rules when you do it honestly. Google's spam policies on link spam cover things like buying or selling links for ranking, excessive link exchanges and automated link creation. Suggesting a relevant replacement that the editor is free to accept or ignore is none of those.

It is not a fast tactic. Many emails go unanswered, and some site owners just delete the dead link. Plan for steady, small wins rather than a sudden jump in links.

Step 1: Pick a niche you can serve well

Start with topics where you already have, or can realistically create, the best page on the web. Broken link building fails when your replacement is weaker than what was lost.

  • List three to five topics your business knows deeply.
  • For each, note the page on your site that could replace a dead resource, or the page you would need to create.
  • Favor evergreen topics (how-to guides, checklists, glossaries, tools). Resource pages link to these far more often than to news or promotions.

A hypothetical bike repair shop might pick "fixing a flat tire", "basic bike maintenance schedule" and "choosing a bike lock". All three are things a school, cycling club or city transport page might list as resources.

Step 2: Find resource pages in your niche

Resource pages are the best hunting ground because their whole job is linking out. Use Google search operators to find them:

  • bike maintenance intitle:resources
  • cycling inurl:links
  • "useful links" bike repair
  • "recommended resources" cycling safety

Look for pages on sites with a real audience: schools, libraries, clubs, local government, associations and established blogs. Skip link farms, pages with hundreds of unrelated links, and anything that looks built only to sell links.

Collect the URLs in a spreadsheet as you go. Fifty relevant resource pages is a good first batch.

Step 3: Crawl those pages to find dead outbound links

Clicking every link by hand does not scale. Instead, crawl the resource pages and check the status code of every outbound link.

Any link checker or crawler that reports the HTTP status code of each outbound link will do. Keep the check limited to the resource page itself rather than the whole site, and run it at a polite speed so you are not hammering someone else's server.

When you review the results, sort dead links into groups:

  • Clear 404 or 410: the page is gone. Best candidates.
  • Domain no longer resolves: the whole site is gone. Also strong candidates.
  • Redirects to an unrelated homepage: technically not broken, but the original resource is lost. Worth checking manually. Our guide to 301 vs 302 redirects explains why these behave differently from a true 404.
  • Timeouts or 5xx errors: could be temporary. Re-check a few days later before contacting anyone.

Before you email anyone, make sure your own house is in order: a site with broken links of its own makes a weak case. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO flags 4xx and 5xx responses and broken links across your site, and our guide on how to find and fix broken links walks through fixing them.

Step 4: Find out what the dead page used to cover

Before you pitch a replacement, you need to know what the original actually offered. The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine is the standard tool for this: enter the dead URL into the Wayback Machine and browse its saved snapshots.

For each dead link, note:

  • The topic and the angle (beginner guide, checklist, tool, research).
  • Roughly how long and detailed it was.
  • Whether other resource pages also link to it. A dead page linked from many places is worth more effort, because one replacement can be pitched to all of them.

Some URLs will have no archived copy. In that case, use the anchor text and the surrounding text on the resource page to work out what it covered.

Step 5: Create or match a replacement

Now compare the dead page with what you have.

  • You already have a close match: make sure it covers everything the original did, and update it if it is thin or out of date.
  • You have something partly related: expand it, or add a section that covers the missing ground.
  • You have nothing: only create a new page if the topic fits your site and you can make it genuinely better. If several dead links point to the same lost resource, the effort is easier to justify.

Do not copy the archived content. It belongs to someone else. Use it to understand the scope, then write your own page with your own examples and knowledge.

Step 6: Write a short, honest outreach email

The email has one job: report the broken link clearly and offer an option, without pressure. Keep it under 120 words. Use the person's name if the site lists it, and send it from a real address at your own domain.

Subject: Broken link on your cycling resources page

Hi Jordan,

I was reading the cycling resources page on the Riverside
Cycle Club site and noticed the "Fixing a flat tire" link
goes to a page that no longer exists (it returns a 404).

If you are looking for a replacement, we have a step-by-step
flat repair guide here: https://example.com/fix-a-flat

Either way, I thought you would want to know about the dead link.

Thanks,
Alex
Example Bike Workshop

What makes this work:

  • The subject line describes the problem, not your request.
  • It names the exact page and the exact dead link, so the reader can verify it in seconds.
  • The suggestion is optional, and the last line makes the email useful even if they ignore it.

Never offer payment or a link swap in exchange. If anyone asks for money to place the link, that is a paid link, and Google asks that paid placements be marked as sponsored links using rel="sponsored". That is no longer broken link building, so walk away.

Step 7: Follow up once, then stop

People are busy and emails get buried. One polite follow-up, about a week after the first email, is reasonable. Keep it to two sentences and reply in the same thread.

After that, stop. Repeated follow-ups turn a helpful note into spam, and a site owner who feels pestered will not link to you.

If someone replies asking you not to contact them, remove them from your list immediately.

Step 8: Track everything in one sheet

A simple spreadsheet keeps you from emailing the same person twice and shows you what is working.

ColumnWhat to record
Resource pageURL of the page with the dead link
Dead linkThe broken URL and its status (404, DNS error, and so on)
Your replacementThe page you suggested
ContactName and email, plus how you found it
Sent / follow-upDates for each
OutcomeLinked, removed dead link, declined, no reply

After your first batch, look at the outcomes. If one type of site (say, school pages) responds much better than others, focus there next time. If nobody links, the replacement pages are usually the issue, not the email.

Ethics: keep it helpful, not spammy

A few rules keep this tactic clean:

  • Only suggest pages that are genuinely relevant and at least as good as what was lost.
  • Send individual emails, not mass blasts with mail-merge placeholders.
  • Do not create fake personas or pretend to be a reader if you are the site owner.
  • Respect a "no" and any request not to be contacted.

Broken link building works best as one part of a wider presence. Being active and useful in the communities your audience already uses, as covered in our guide to earning mentions through online communities, makes your name familiar before your email ever lands.

The bottom line

Broken link building turns outreach around: you start by reporting a real problem and offering a real fix. The process is simple (find resource pages, crawl them for dead links, check what was lost, build something better, send a short email), but it rewards patience and quality over volume.

Expect most emails to go unanswered and treat every link you do earn as a sign your content is genuinely useful. Keep it honest, keep it relevant, and never pay or trade for the link.

Your next step: find ten resource pages in your niche with the search operators above, crawl them for 404s, and write down which dead links your existing content could already replace.

faqs.question: Is broken link building still effective?
faqs.answer: It can be, as long as your replacement content is genuinely relevant and useful. Many emails will not get a reply, so it works best as a steady, long-term tactic rather than a quick win. Quality of the replacement page matters more than the number of emails sent.

faqs.question: Is broken link building against Google's guidelines?
faqs.answer: Suggesting a relevant replacement that the site owner is free to accept is not link spam. It becomes a problem if you pay for the link, set up link swaps, or use automated programs or services to create links. Paid placements should be marked with rel=sponsored.

faqs.question: How do I find broken links on other websites?
faqs.answer: Find resource pages with search operators such as intitle:resources or inurl:links plus your topic, then crawl those pages and check the status code of each outbound link. Links that return 404, 410 or point to domains that no longer exist are the strongest candidates.

faqs.question: How many follow-up emails should I send?
faqs.answer: One follow-up, about a week after the first email, is enough. More than that tends to annoy site owners and makes your outreach look like spam. Always stop if someone asks you not to contact them again.
